content:
With Apple set to roll out its 2027 system versions, the WebKit blog recently published an in-depth article detailing the new features of Safari 27.0. Here's a summary of the contents.

Safari MCP server is the standout new feature

Among the new features in Safari 27.0, the most eye-catching is undoubtedly the Safari MCP server, which enables AI agents to control the browser window and helps developers work more efficiently.

To enable Safari MCP, developers need to go to "Safari > Settings > Developer" and tick "Allow remote automation and external agents." Apple reminds users that the Developer panel will only appear after the user has enabled "Show features for web developers" under "Safari > Settings > Advanced."

Below is Apple's introduction to this new feature:

Are you using a coding agent to build your website? Safari 27.0 brings you the new Safari MCP server, making your workflow faster and more powerful. Let Claude Code, Codex, or your favourite agent take control of the browser window to see your code rendered in real time. Safari MCP gives you access to the DOM, network requests, screenshots, and console output. Your agent can do more on its own, so you won't have to keep switching windows, pasting screenshots into the terminal, or repeatedly typing prompts to explain what's going wrong. The Safari MCP server lets your agent: see how your code renders in Safari; verify user states for forms, checkout flows, selections, and more; compare computed styles and layouts against the results in other browsers; test accessibility issues such as missing labels, improperly set ARIA attributes, and insufficient contrast; analyse performance metrics like load times and resource fetch times; and much more. The MCP server runs entirely on-device, doesn't make its own network requests, can't access your personal data in Safari, and only sends the data it captures to the agent you're working with — not to Apple.

Apple's blog post also lists the specific commands developers need to use to connect Claude Code, Codex, or other agents to Safari, and welcomes feedback and feature suggestions from developers.

In addition to MCP support, Safari 27.0 has also fixed nearly 850 issues, more than the 525 fixes Apple announced at WWDC a few months ago. The fixed issues span multiple areas including accessibility, CSS, encoding, fonts, forms, MathML, networking, and WebRTC.

Safari 27.0 also adds support for immersive environments, allowing developers to deliver related experiences on visionOS, and extends the HTML <model> element to iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, enabling websites to embed interactive 3D models directly within a page, used in a manner similar to images or videos.

The article also introduces the brand-new (and quite practical) "scroll anchoring" feature, which prevents the page from jumping when images load above the content the user is currently reading, while listing a number of Web Inspector improvements, including inline colour contrast information, a clearer view of redirect chains, and enhanced layout debugging capabilities.

The list also details improvements and new features in areas such as WebAssembly, WebGPU, JavaScript, CSS, WebRTC, media playback, Web Extensions, WKWebView, and Service Workers. The full article can be read here.
